beforeCard.prompt: Если вы не уверены, разрешено ли в парке собирать найденные раковины или камни, как поступить?

answers.text: Забрать находку, если она выглядит обычной и лежит свободно.
answers.note: Даже обычный природный объект занимает своё место; некоторые категории находок отдельно защищены законом.

answers.text: Переложить её ближе к тропе, чтобы другие посетители тоже заметили находку.
answers.note: Камни могут служить укрытием организмам и удерживать воду именно там, где лежат.

answers.text: Оставить её на месте и при сомнении уточнить правила у рейнджера.
answers.note: Некоторые находки можно собирать лишь в определённых местах и количествах; это уточняют в правилах парка или у рейнджера.

answers.text: Взять одну, если вокруг много похожих предметов.
answers.note: Даже разрешённый сбор может зависеть от места и количества, а не от того, много ли похожих находок вокруг.

L19: # I Didn't Know That!: Leave No Trace Principle #4 - Leave What You Find
L20: 
L21: cite1†Image: Leave What You Find L22: 
L23: You’re walking down a trail and come upon a brilliantly colored and intricately patterned rock. It’s gorgeous! You want to take it home to show your nephew. Then maybe you’ll find a place for it on your desk to remember this amazing trip. You reach down to pick it up to stow it away in your pocket. But wait!
L24: cite2†Image: River rocks Riverbeds are often full of fascinating finds, like these intricate river rocks.
L25: 
L26: NPS Photo
L27: 
L28: The natural world is full of fascinating finds that awe us with their beauty and intrigue. From colorful rocks and seashells to artifacts, feathers, and fossils. While you may be tempted to bring these items home with you, please leave them where you find them.
L29: #### Did You Know?
L30: 
L31: Leave what you find is one of the 7 Leave No Trace Principles. These Principles empower you to leave nature as unchanged by your presence as possible. It’s a way of protecting the natural world and yourself and to preserve our outdoor spaces for the enjoyment of generations to come.
L32: 
L33: cite3†Image: Super Bloom - Death Valley 2019 super bloom in Death Valley National Park.
L34: 
L35: NPS / Kurt Moses
L36: ## A Part of the Experience
L37: Finding “treasures” in the natural world is part of the experience of exploring our protected places. With over 300 million visitors to parks each year, if everyone took something, it would leave a huge impact! And it would alter the experience for everyone. Imagine visiting Petrified Forest National Park and seeing no petrified wood. Or going to see a “super bloom” in Death Valley National Park and finding no flowers.
L38: Every item removed from its place also removes a piece of that place for future visitors. Leave what you find and let others experience the same sense of wonder and discovery that you felt when you found a “treasure” in the natural world.
L39: cite4†Image: petrified wood A colorful piece of petrified wood found at Petrified Forest National Park.
L40: 
L41: NPS Photo
L42: ## Role of Natural Items
L43: 
L44: The items we find in nature have a role to play, either in the ecosystem or the story of the landscape. Leaving what we find in place helps to preserve both.
L45: 
L46: All natural items play a role in their ecosystems. For example, flowers are more than just beautiful. They are also important sources of pollen for pollinators. And, if fertilized, they become seeds or fruit, which could be food for other animals or become new flowers!
L47: Even dead things have a role to play! For example, dead leaves and sticks might seem to have no purpose, but they actually play a big role. They can provide cover for amphibians, reptiles, insects, and even pollinators. Birds can use them to build their nests. And as they decompose, they also recycle nutrients back into the soil.
L48: 
L49: cite5†Image: Bighorn sheep skull A bighorn sheep skull in Glacier National Park.
L50: 
L51: NPS Photo
L52: ### But it's just a...
L53: 
L54: Click through the drop down boxes below to find out what roles these items play in their ecosystems.
L55: #### [Button: Rock ]
L56: 
L57:   * Soil formation: Rocks weather over time to create soil, which provides a medium for plants to grow and supports diverse communities of organisms, from fungi to insects.
L58: 
L59:   * Habitat and shelter: Rocks provide habitat and shelter for a variety of organisms, particularly in rocky habitats such as shorelines and mountainsides. Organisms may use rocks as protection from predators, for thermal regulation (to keep cool or warm), or as a surface to attach to.
L60:   * Water retention: Rocks can help to retain water in the soil, reducing erosion and providing a more stable environment for plants and other organisms.
L61: 
L62:   * Nutrient cycling: When rocks weather, they release nutrients into the soil that can be taken up by plants.
L63: 
L64:   * Geological diversity: Rocks provide geological diversity and contribute to the unique characteristics of ecosystems. Rocks tell a story of the geologic past.
L65: #### [Button: Feather ]
L66: 
L67:   * Nesting material: Feathers are often used as a material for building nests, providing a warm and soft environment for young birds to grow and develop.
L68: 
L69:   * Decomposition: When birds molt or die, their feathers decompose and release nutrients back into the ecosystem. This helps to keep the soil fertile and support other organisms in the food chain.
L70: #### [Button: Shed Antlers ]
L71: 
L72:   * Nutrient cycling: Shed antlers, like other bone material, are composed of a variety of essential nutrients and minerals which can be slowly released into the ecosystem as the antlers decompose. This process helps to keep soil fertile and support the growth of plants and other organisms.
L73:   * Chewing: Shed antlers are an important source of calcium and phosphorus. Many animals chew on them for nutrients or to sharpen teeth.
L74:   * Stimulation: Wolves have been known to cite6†bring antlers back to their pups as "toys."†www.facebook.com L75: #### [Button: Flower ]
L76: 
L77:   * Reproduction and pollination: Flowers are the reproductive organs of plants, and they produce nectar and pollen to attract pollinators like bees, butterflies, and birds. Pollinators assist in the transfer of genetic material between plants, which allows for plant reproduction and genetic diversity.
L78:   * Food and habitat: Flowers provide food for insects, such as bees and butterflies, as well as larger animals like birds and bats that may consume the nectar and pollen. The flowers also provide habitat for numerous insects and other invertebrates that live among the petals and leaves.
L79: 
L80:   * Beauty and aesthetics: Flowers contribute to the overall beauty and richness of the natural world.
L81: #### [Button: Pine Cone ]
L82: 
L83:   * Seed dispersal: Pine cones are full of seeds that are dispersed by birds, squirrels, and other animals that eat or carry them away from the parent tree. This helps to maintain genetic diversity in the ecosystem and allows for the expansion of new populations of pine trees.
L84: 
L85:   * Nutrient cycling: When pine cones fall to the ground and decompose, they release nutrients into the soil that can be taken up by other plants. This helps to maintain soil fertility in the ecosystem.
L86:   * Habitat and shelter: Pine cones can provide habitat and shelter for a variety of organisms. For example, some species of birds use pine cones as nesting material, while others may use them for cover or protection from predators.
L87: #### [Button: Dead Leaf ]
L88: 
L89:   * Nutrient cycling: Dead leaves decompose and release their nutrients back into the soil, where they can be taken up by other plants. This helps to maintain soil fertility in the ecosystem.
L90: 
L91:   * Habitat and shelter: Dead leaves provide habitat and shelter for a variety of organisms, including insects, fungi, and small mammals.
L92:   * Water retention: Dead leaves help to retain moisture in the soil, reducing erosion and providing a more stable environment for plants and other organisms.
L93: 
L94:   * Carbon sequestration: Dead leaves and other plant material can sequester carbon in the soil, helping to reduce the amount of carbon in the atmosphere.
L95: #### [Button: Empty Bird Nest ]
L96: 
L97:   * Shelter and habitat: Empty bird nests can provide shelter and habitat for a variety of organisms, including insects, small mammals, and other birds. Some species of birds, such as owls and woodpeckers, may use old nests as roosting sites or as a temporary refuge.
L98: 
L99:   * Signaling and behavior: Some bird species may use old nests as signaling devices to mark territories or attract mates.
L100:   * They're often reused! Many species of birds, including house sparrows, wrens, and common starlings, save time and energy by using old and abandoned nests as their own.
L101: ## Role of Cultural Items and Artifacts
L102: 
L103: Just as with natural items, it is important to leave cultural items and artifacts where you find them. These items, and their original locations, tell us a story of our shared heritage. When they are taken, that story is harder to piece together. These items are sometimes sacred or extremely meaningful to specific cultures and communities and are often irreplaceable.
L104: #### What do I do if I find an artifact?
L105: 
L106:   1. Leave it be! Don’t pick it up or move it in any way.
L107: 
L108:   2. Document the location. Note where you are. Snap a picture of the artifact where you found it. Step back and photograph the artifact with a landmark.
L109: 
L110:   3. Alert a park ranger. Show a park ranger your pictures and the location of the artifact. If you cannot find a ranger, visit the park website and click the “Contact Us” link at the bottom the page.
L111: cite7†Image: pottery shards Pot shards at Petrified Forest National Park.
L112: 
L113: NPS Photo
L114: ## It’s the Law
L115: 
L116: Leaving what you find isn’t just good etiquette, it’s also the law—especially on federal lands.
L117: 
L118: Archeological items are protected by a law called the Archeological Resources Protection Act (ARPA).
L119: Many natural items are also protected by law. For example, the Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act prohibits anyone without a permit from taking bald or golden eagles, including their parts (feathers, skulls, etc.), nests, or eggs. The Migratory Bird Treaty Act provides similar protections to listed migratory birds.
L120: 
L121: Here are just a few other laws that help preserve and protect our natural and cultural resources.
L122:   * NPS Organic Act of 1916
L123:   * Code of Federal Regulations § 2.1 Preservation of natural, cultural and archeological resources
L124:   * Antiquities Act of 1906
L125:   * Federal Cave Resources Protection Act
L126:   * National Historic Preservation Act
L127:   * Wilderness Act
L128:   * The Paleontological Resources Preservation Act (PRPA)
L129: #### Check the Compendium!
L130: 
L131: Some natural items like berries, nuts, firewood, or unoccupied seashells, may be gathered in certain areas and in certain quantities. Check the Superintendent’s Compendium for the park that you are visiting (often available on park websites) for specific regulations related to collecting natural resources. Or ask a park ranger. When in doubt, leave it be!
L132: cite8†Image: Antler selfie! A hiker chooses to take home a photo memory rather than taking a moose antler from Denali National Park.
L133: 
L134: NPS / Emily Mesner
L135: ## What You Can Do
L136: 
L137: Leaving what you find doesn’t have to put a damper on your outdoor experience. There are many ways to appreciate and enjoy found items without disturbing them or taking them with you. Here are some ways you can enjoy nature’s treasures in a low impact way.
L138: 
L139:   * Bring a camera and take pictures
L140: 
L141:   * Bring a field guide to identify flowers, plants, and mushrooms
L142: 
L143:   * Leave cultural artifacts where you found them and tell a park ranger
L144:   * Start a nature journal and record, make sketches, and write about what you find
L145: 
L146:   * Do a photo scavenger hunt, where you take pictures of what you find instead of collecting the items
L147: 
L148:   * Learn more about the fourth Leave No Trace Principle, Leave What You Find
L149: 
L150: cite9†Image: Nature Journal Starting a nature journal is a great way to capture memories of what you find while exploring nature.
L151: 
L152: NPS Photo
L153: ## Pass It On!
L154: 
L155: Did you learn something new? Pass it on! Protecting our ecosystems and historic artifacts is a job for us all, but there’s no way for everyone to be an expert in everything. That’s why sharing knowledge is so important!
L156: Download or screenshot this card to share with a friend or help spread the word and encourage others to Leave No Trace by leaving what you find so that everyone can enjoy the treasures that nature has to offer. Thank you for helping protect our natural spaces for generations to come.
L157:

L30: NPS Photo
L31: ### Fun Now and Fun Later
L32: Look at the picture to the right. You will see a youth group and chaperone having fun tubing in the Potomac River at the C&O Canal. They are able to swim and enjoy the river because NPS staff monitor and manage water quality standards. Making sure the Potomac River and other bodies of water are preserved and protected is important for recreation at the NPS.
L33: Stewardship of your National Parks helps ensure we can have fun now and even more fun in the future. The trails you bike on sunny days are possible because of park stewards and everyday citizens – like you! In this activity module, you will learn how stewardship helps fuel recreation and what you can do to help.
L34: cite3†Image: Imagine L35: ## #RecreateResponsibly
L36: ### Leave No Trace
L37: Imagine you are hiking a trail with a few friends. Your group notices some trash and litter along the side of the towpath. How do you think waste impacts your environment? Does it make your trip even a little less enjoyable? Practicing the 7 Leave No Trace (LNT) principles is an important duty for all Canal Stewards. The LNT principles guide you to recreate sustainably in your National Parks. Review the 7 principles below then test your skills by playing cite4†Leave No Trace Charades with friends!
L38: #### cite5†Principle #1 – Plan Ahead and Prepare L39: 
L40:   * Know the regulations and special concerns for the area you'll visit.
L41:   * Prepare for extreme weather, hazards, and emergencies.
L42:   * Schedule your trip to avoid times of high use.
L43:   * Visit in small groups when possible. Consider splitting larger groups into smaller groups.
L44:   * Repackage food to minimize waste.
L45:   * Use a map and compass or GPS to eliminate the use of marking paint, rock cairns, or flagging.
L46: #### cite6†Principle #2 – Travel and Camp on Durable Surfaces L47:   * Durable surfaces include maintained trails and designated campsites, rock, gravel, sand, dry grasses or snow.
L48:   * Protect riparian areas by camping at least 200 feet from lakes and streams.
L49:   * Good campsites are found, not made. Altering a site is not necessary.
L50:     * In popular areas:
L51:       * Concentrate use on existing trails and campsites.
L52:       * Walk single file in the middle of the trail, even when wet or muddy.
L53:       * Keep campsites small. Focus activity in areas where vegetation is absent.
L54:     * In pristine areas:
L55:       * Disperse use to prevent the creation of campsites and trails.
L56:       * Avoid places where impacts are just beginning.
L57: #### cite7†Principle #3 – Dispose of Waste Properly L58:   * Pack it in, pack it out. Inspect your campsite, food preparation areas, and rest areas for trash or spilled foods. Pack out all trash, leftover food and litter.
L59:   * Utilize toilet facilities whenever possible. Otherwise, deposit solid human waste in catholes dug 6 to 8 inches deep, at least 200 feet from water, camp and trails. Cover and disguise the cathole when finished.
L60:   * Pack out toilet paper and hygiene products.
L61:   * To wash yourself or your dishes, carry water 200 feet away from streams or lakes and use small amounts of biodegradable soap. Scatter strained dishwater.
L62: #### cite8†Principle #4 – Leave What You Find L63: 
L64:   * Preserve the past: examine, photograph, but do not touch cultural or historic structures and artifacts.
L65:   * Leave rocks, plants and other natural objects as you find them.
L66:   * Avoid introducing or transporting non-native species.
L67:   * Do not build structures, furniture, or dig trenches.
L68: #### cite9†Principle #5 – Minimize Campfire Impacts L69: 
L70:   * Campfires can cause lasting impacts to the environment. Use a lightweight stove for cooking and enjoy a candle lantern for light.
L71:   * Where fires are permitted, use established fire rings, fire pans, or mound fires.
L72:   * Keep fires small. Only use down and dead wood from the ground that can be broken by hand.
L73:   * Burn all wood and coals to ash, put out campfires completely, then scatter cool ashes.
L74: #### cite10†Principles #6 – Respect Wildlife L75: 
L76:   * Observe wildlife from a distance. Do not follow or approach them.
L77:   * Never feed animals. Feeding wildlife damages their health, alters natural behaviors, [habituates them to humans], and exposes them to predators and other dangers.
L78:   * Protect wildlife and your food by storing rations and trash securely.
L79:   * Control pets at all times, or leave them at home.
L80:   * Avoid wildlife during sensitive times: mating, nesting, raising young, or winter.
L81: #### cite11†Principles #7 – Be Considerate of Others L82: 
L83:   * Respect other visitors and protect the quality of their experience.
L84:   * Be courteous. Yield to other users on the trail.
L85:   * Step to the downhill side of the trail when encountering pack stock.
L86:   * Take breaks and camp away from trails and other visitors.
L87:   * Let nature's sounds prevail. Avoid loud voices and noises.

L92: ### cite12†Keep Safety In the Picture L93: 
L94: Make your trip to a national park a fun and memorable experience for the whole family. Learn how to safely watch and photography wildlife, best time, and how to find the picture perfect location for the best shot! When capturing precious moments, be a smart photographer and follow these picture-perfect tips from the National Park Service.

L100: cite17†Image: Outdoor Fun L101: ## Practice Your Skills
L102: Get ready to put your stewardship and Leave No Trace skills to the test with one of these outdoor challenges! There are a plethora of ways to combine your interests of recreation and the outdoors at the C&O Canal. Complete 1 (or more!) of the outdoor adventures below. Connect with us on our social media accounts using the hashtag #CanalKidsVJR to share your park adventure as you discover the connections of recreation in stewardship.
L103: Begin by clicking one of the activity titles, then follow the links for specific directions.
L104: #### cite18†Play these Trail Games L105: 
L106: Start here ⇒ cite19†Trail Games L107: Trail games are a great way to break up your hike or just have fun on the towpath! Take a water break, stretch, and try some of these trail games the next time you visit the C&O Canal National Historical Park. Remember to cite20†#RecreateResponsibly and cite21†Leave No Trace while having fun in the Park.
L108: #### cite22†Find a TRACK Trail Near You L109: 
L110: Find two TRACK Trails in Williamsport, MD. Each trail is about one mile roundtrip. TRACK Trails, part of Kids in Parks, provides family-friendly trails to get kids outdoors and connected with nature.
L111:

L116: Get started here ⇒ cite26†Family Biking Trips L117: Let's go ride a bike on the C&O Canal towpath! Another great way to explore the towpath is on a bicycle with family and friends. There are many places you can access the canal to explore up and down river. Many cite27†Canal Towns†www.canaltrust.org offer bike rental shops.

L124: ## cite29†Every Kid Outdoors†everykidoutdoors.gov L125: 
L126: Hey fourth graders! See America's natural wonders and historic sites with your family for free with the Every Kid Outdoors program. cite30†Get a voucher pass†everykidoutdoors.gov that admits the 4th grader, other children, and up to 3 adults. Bring your voucher when you visit the Great Falls area of the C&O Canal.
L127: ## cite31†Let's Move Outside†letsmove.obamawhitehouse.archives.gov L128: 
L129: Did you know that 60 minutes of daily active play outdoors keeps your body healthy? Let's Move Outside encourages you to stay active in your local National Parks. Ride a bike, take a walk, or go for a run along the towpath to stay healthy!

L136: ## cite33†Passport to Your National Parks: Virtual Cancellation Hub†americasnationalparks.org L137:

L158: ## cite39†Yoga Hike L159: 
L160: Combining art, movement, and meditation, a yoga hike is an easy way to connect in National Parks and with nature around you! Slow yourself down with a reflective hike at the C&O Canal National Historical Park. Benefits from walking the C&O Canal are endless!
